[1] Defense White Paper Ministry of National Defense Publisher's Note The rapidly changing security environment, both domestically and internationally, presents us with new challenges and opportunities

[2] Globally, transnational and non-military threats, such as international terrorism and weapons of mass destruction, are rapidly spreading, raising the need for an international cooperative system to respond

[3] Furthermore, in Northeast Asia, economic cooperation and interdependence are increasing, while political and military conflicts and factors of conflict persist, resulting in an uncertain and fluid security situation

[4] Meanwhile, inter-Korean relations are advancing through exchanges and cooperation, including the construction of the Kaesong Industrial Complex, the inter-Korean railway and road connection project, and Mount Kumgang tourism

[5] Despite this progress, North Korea's military threat remains unchanged on the Korean Peninsula, and the North Korean nuclear issue is emerging as the greatest threat to our national security

[6] This creates a dual situation of military confrontation and tension

[7] Domestically, with the realignment and reduction of USFK forces in response to shifts in US global strategy, there is a growing demand for the development of a future-oriented ROK-US alliance and an expanded role for our military in defending the Korean Peninsula

[8] To overcome these diverse challenges and threats and leverage them as opportunities to maintain and develop a stronger national defense, we need a new paradigm shift beyond the existing framework of national defense, along with more proactive and active efforts

[9] Defense White Paper

[10] Accordingly, our military is establishing a perfect national defense posture, built on the foundation of a robust ROK-US alliance, capable of responding to any type of threat

[11] We are also steadily pursuing cooperative and self-reliant defense to strengthen our absolute security capabilities by rapidly expanding our war deterrence

[12] Furthermore, we are continuously pursuing defense reform based on a new defense paradigm to meet the demands of "change and innovation," achieve advanced and modernized national defense operations, and establish a trustworthy ROK military

[13] Our military clearly recognizes that "the source of national defense power comes from the people," and by dedicating itself to its fundamental mission and mission, we will realize a "robust national defense that stands with the people

[14] The "2004 Defense White Paper" was written to honestly inform the public of these efforts

[15] This White Paper details changes in the security situation, the direction of national defense policy and posture, the current status and tasks of our national defense, the direction of defense reform to efficiently operate national defense, and the military's activities to promote public convenience and protect the rights and interests of the people as a "military that stands with the people

[16] In particular, it details the current status and future direction of the realignment of US Forces Korea, which is underway amidst public concern and interest, and the activities and achievements of the Zaytun Unit, which has been deployed to Iraq and is successfully carrying out its mission to support peace and reconstruction

[17] Furthermore, various materials have been compiled and attached as appendices to facilitate in-depth understanding and research in the field of security

[18] We hope this Defense White Paper will be of great help in broadening the public's understanding and sympathy for national defense policy, and we ask for your continued support and interest in national defense. [106] Changes and Challenges in the Security Environment Section 1 Global Security Situation Section 2 Northeast Asian Security Situation Section 3 North Korean Situation and Military Threats Chapter 1: Changes and Challenges in the Security Environment Today, the international security situation is experiencing a surge of conflicts stemming from issues such as territorial, religious, resource, environmental, and ethnic issues that were latent during the Cold War

[107] International terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction are emerging as serious threats to the stability and peace of the international community

[108] Since the September 11 attacks, the United States has been leading the restructuring of the world order around counterterrorism and the non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction

[109] It has also employed preemptive strikes and selective intervention strategies to prevent and deter international terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction

[110] Meanwhile, closer international cooperation is required at the global level to address the proliferation of various transnational and non-military threats, such as terrorism, international crime, and illicit arms trafficking

[111] Therefore, active international efforts are being made to maintain international peace and resolve conflicts

[112] Proliferation of New Threats A. Terrorism In 2001, the United States September 11 terrorist attacks demonstrated that even a superpower like the United States can suffer property and human losses comparable to wartime, and be gripped by shock and a sense of crisis bordering on psychological panic, all due to a single terrorist organization

[113] This led to the recognition of the unpredictable threat of terrorism from non-state organizations and forces as a critical area of national security

[114] Today, terrorism is characterized by forces transcending territories and borders, interconnected through a global network, making it difficult to identify its true nature and unpredictable in time and location

[115] The transnational terrorist threat, scattered throughout the world, has fundamentally altered the traditional concepts of enemies and threats, as well as the concept of preparedness against such threats

[116] Along with international terrorism, the development and proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (WMD), including nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons, by certain states and terrorist groups are considered major threats to global security

[117] Some countries, including North Korea, Iran, and Syria, have developed nuclear and They possess the technology to develop missiles, and the components and materials needed for development can be easily obtained through international black market transactions

[118] Furthermore, biochemical weapons such as anthrax and sarin gas are easy to manufacture and inexpensive to produce, making them easily accessible not only to many weaker nations but also to terrorist organizations

[119] Therefore, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their potential use by international terrorist organizations pose a serious threat to global security

[120] Therefore, the international community is strengthening efforts to eliminate the production capabilities of WMDs in countries with proliferation concerns and to prevent their proliferation

[121] WMD: Weapons of Mass Destruction Regional instability and the persistence of local conflicts

[122] Due to complex conflict factors such as territorial and resource disputes, religious, racial, and ethnic conflicts, and separatist movements that were latent during the Cold War, various forms of local conflicts are on the rise around the world

[123] In 2004 alone, 28 conflicts occurred in Africa, including the Sudanese Civil War; five in the Americas, including the Colombian Civil War; and three in the Middle East

[124] There have been 13 such incidents in Asia, including the Iraq War, 20 such incidents in Asia, including the Nepalese civil war, 9 such incidents in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), including the Russian-Chechen conflict, and 9 such incidents in Europe, including the Kosovo War of Independence

[125] There have been constant local conflicts, large and small, throughout the world

[126] CIS: Commonwealth of Independent States A federation of nations established in December 1991 by 12 former Soviet republics, excluding the three Baltic states, following the collapse of the Soviet Union

[127] In particular, since the September 11 terrorist attacks, terrorist activities in Central Asia and Southeast Asia have emerged as a major variable undermining regional stability

[128] Bali bombings Transnational Threats: Threats posed by state or non-state actors that transcend national borders

[129] With the rapid development and proliferation of advanced technologies and information and communication technologies, globalization has accelerated, deepening interdependence between nations and weakening the concept of national borders, leading to increased risk of international crime, piracy, and Transnational and non-military threats, such as illegal refugees and cyberterrorism, are diverse

[130] Non-military threats: Threats posed by state and non-state actors through means other than military force or by natural factors

[131] Defense White Paper 19 Chapter 1: Changes and Challenges in the Security Environment Defense White Paper are emerging in various forms

[132] The recent large-scale earthquake and tsunami in Southeast Asia, as well as large-scale natural disasters and environmental pollution exacerbated by global warming, as well as emerging infectious diseases such as AIDS and severe acute respiratory syndrome, are emerging as new forms of security threats

[133] Furthermore, as the actors involved in security-related activities diversify, not only individual states but also terrorist groups, criminal organizations, religious groups, ethnic groups, and various non-governmental organizations are emerging as key actors in international politics

[134] International Efforts for Peace and Stability A. Conflict Resolution Efforts by International Organizations, including the United Nations Various forms of regional conflicts and transnational non-military threats increase, the role of the UN, various international organizations, and regional multilateral security cooperation organizations in preventing and resolving them is becoming increasingly important

[135] Accordingly, the UN's areas of activity are expanding to include disarmament, development, the environment, human rights, and narcotics

[136] Peacekeeping operations are also becoming increasingly diverse, encompassing conflict prevention, fostering an environment conducive to peace negotiations, monitoring the implementation of comprehensive agreements, delivering humanitarian aid, and enforcing ceasefire agreements

[137] However, as seen in conflicts in the Middle East and Africa, when the interests of the permanent members of the Security Council conflict or when international consensus fails to emerge among major powers, the UN's ability to resolve conflicts is inevitably limited

[138] Member states recognize the need for the UN to become a more effective organization to reflect the new international reality

[139] However, disagreements remain over whether to expand the Security Council, which is charged with ensuring international peace and security, and particularly the issue of granting it veto power, due to conflicting opinions among member states

[140] Regional Security Cooperation System Development With the UN's role in resolving international disputes insufficient, the importance of multilateral regional security cooperation organizations is growing

[141] In the Asia-Pacific region, the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) has served as a venue for various consultations since 1994 Section 1: Global Security Situation building trust and promoting preventive diplomacy within the region

[142] With North Korea's accession in July 2000, it is establishing itself as the only intergovernmental multilateral security cooperation system in the Asia-Pacific region

[143] At the Foreign Ministers' Meeting held in July 2004, measures for international cooperation to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and counterterrorism were discussed

[144] The ARF, along with the ASEAN+3 and APEC summits, is expected to contribute to regional stability as it serves as an annual forum for formal and informal contact between participating countries on regional security issues

[145] However, due to the diverse political and ethnic backgrounds and interests of the participating countries, substantial time and effort are needed to fully realize security cooperation functions

[146] In Europe, regional security cooperation is being strengthened, including through the expansion of the political, diplomatic, and military roles of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and the European Union (EU), in parallel with existing cooperation through the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE

[147] NATO expanded to 26 countries on March 29, 2004, with the addition of seven new Eastern European countries, and is seeking to expand its defense role beyond Europe

[148] The EU expanded to 25 member states on May 1, 2004, and is pursuing counter-terrorism cooperation measures, including establishing an information-sharing system among member states, blocking terrorist financing and asset freezing, strengthening border controls, and establishing a counter-terrorism database

[149] In Africa, the African Union (AU) was established on May 26, 2001, to mediate regional conflicts and represent the interests of the entire continent

[150] On February 3, 2003, the AU Summit agreed to establish a Peace and Security Commission with the authority to directly intervene in armed conflicts

[151] Currently, the AU is being promoted as a regional integration body similar to the EU, to address the post-Cold War decline in international economic support and the trend toward regional economic blocs

[152] However, the AU faces challenges such as conflicting interests among some member states, such as South Africa and Libya, member states' reluctance to cede sovereignty, and securing large operating funds

[153] ASEAN Regional Forum

[154] Association of South-East Asian Nations APEC: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ASEAN+3: Korea, China, Japan OSCE: Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe NATO: North Atlantic Treaty Organization EU: European Union AU: African Union C. Strategic Arms Reduction and Efforts to Prevent the Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction On May 24, 2002, the United States and Russia signed the Treaty on the Reduction of Strategic Nuclear Arms (Moscow Treaty), pledging to reduce the number of nuclear warheads in both countries to 1,700–2,200 by the end of December 2012 and to maintain the composition and structure of their nuclear forces within this upper limit

[155] The Moscow Treaty was ratified by the U.S. Senate in March 2003 and by the Russian Senate and House of Representatives in May

[156] It entered into force in June 2003 after the exchange of instruments of ratification at the U.S.-Russia Summit

[157] Chapter 1: Changes and Challenges in the Security Environment

[158] By allowing each country to independently decide within the scope of its nuclear weapons program, the United States is actively pursuing large-scale nuclear arms reductions

[159] Meanwhile, the United States is deeply concerned about the risk of the development and proliferation of weapons of mass destruction by countries such as North Korea and Iran, and the transfer of weapons of mass destruction held by these countries to international terrorist organizations

[160] Accordingly, the United States is actively promoting the Proliferation Security Initiative (PSI), which aims to block the trade in weapons of mass destruction by sea, air, and land as part of the establishment of an international cooperation system to control the transfer of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery

[161] Since hosting the first PSI meeting (with 11 participating countries, currently 15), in Madrid in June 2003, the United States has conducted seven PSI meetings and 12 PSI exercises as of the end of 2004, including joint maritime exercises among PSI participating countries

[162] Furthermore, on September 23, 2003, President Bush authorized the OPSI exercise (Tracking of Ships Suspected of Loading Weapons of Mass Destruction

[163] PSI: Proliferation Security Initiatives

[164] UN Security Council Resolution 1540 Non-state actors, including international terrorist organizations, develop and use nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons and their means of delivery

[165] Security Council resolutions adopted to prevent the manufacture, possession, transport, transfer, or use of weapons of mass destruction

[166] In his address to the UN General Assembly, he emphasized the need to adopt a UN resolution to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and the UN Security Council unanimously adopted UN Security Council Resolution 1540 on April

[167] Thus, the United States is pressuring countries such as North Korea and Iran to abandon their nuclear development to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, while focusing on expanding the PSI participation and securing global support, including from the UN. A representative example of the US's success in preventing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction after the September 11 terrorist attacks CWC: Chemical Weapons Convention BWC: Biological Weapons Convention The Convention was established in Libya

[168] A prime example is the declaration of abandonment of weapons of mass destruction on December

[169] In this declaration, Libya pledged to completely dismantle all weapons of mass destruction, allow inspections by international organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), simultaneously dismantle missiles exceeding the allowable scope of the Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR), and comply with international disarmament agreements such as the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), and the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC

[170] The United States and the United Kingdom pledged to gradually lift economic sanctions and improve relations based on Libya's performance and level of cooperation in implementing its commitment to abandon weapons of mass destruction

[171] Libya's abandonment of its weapons of mass destruction is considered an example of how the issue of weapons of mass destruction can be resolved peacefully through dialogue and diplomacy

[172] Changing Patterns of War Section 1: Global Security Situation Epochal Advances in Science and Technology With the development of the military, the nature of war is also rapidly changing

[173] The recent wars in Afghanistan and Iraq are prime examples

[174] From the outset, the United States implemented "New Decision Operations (RDO)", which combined large-scale airstrikes using missiles and air power with ground warfare

[175] Furthermore, by effectively utilizing precision strike weapons to minimize unnecessary mass destruction and achieve war objectives early, the United States successfully concluded major operations early by applying the concepts of "Effects-Based Operations (EBO)" and "Network-Centric Operations (NCW)", which efficiently connect combat organizations through networks to enhance combat capabilities

[176] This suggests a shift in the nature of future warfare from one centered on securing territory and inflicting mass casualties and destruction through mass forces and conventional weapons to one centered on utilizing advanced weapon systems such as Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) systems and long-range Precision Strike Weapons (PGM) to paralyze enemy information systems and strike at strategic centers of gravity, thereby annihilating their will to fight

[177] Accordingly, each country is To build military capabilities suited to the new warfare landscape, the ROK is focusing on modernizing and elevating its military power based on available military technology and national capabilities

[178] This is transforming the military from a troop- and equipment-centric to an information- and knowledge-centric, technology-intensive one

[179] Efforts are also being made to strengthen early warning and surveillance, mobility, and precision strike capabilities

[180] RDO: Rapid Decisive Operation EBO: Effect-Based Operation NCW: Network Centric Warfare ISR: Intelligence Surveillance Reconnaissance PGM: Precision Guided Munitions

[181] Precision Guided Munitions Strategic Center: The location, capability, or characteristics where a unit generates freedom of action, tangible combat power, or the will to fight

[182] Chapter

[183] Changes and Challenges in the Security Environment Section

[184] Northeast Asian Security Situation Amidst the global trend of easing tensions and increasing cooperation since the end of the Cold War, Northeast Asia has also experienced economic growth

[185] Cooperative relationships and interdependence are deepening

[186] Measures to enhance economic cooperation through FTAs between regional countries are under discussion, and multilateral security cooperation is being strengthened through ASEAN+3, ARF, and APEC

[187] However, the Cold War structure still lingers in Northeast Asia, and regional conflicts persist, including the North Korean nuclear issue, crossstrait disputes, and potential island and territorial disputes

[188] Furthermore, amidst ongoing competition among countries to expand their influence in a region where the world's largest military forces are concentrated, each country is continuously modernizing its military and pursuing military transformation efforts

[189] US defense policy and strategy: Presented through the Quadrennial Defense Review (2001 QDR: September 30, 2001), the National Security Strategy (NSS: September 20, 2002), and the Annual Report (November 25, 2003). The four major defense objectives of the US: Based on the 2004 National Military Strategy (NMS). Defense policies and military trends in neighboring countries: A. United States Defense Policy To effectively address diverse and uncertain future threats, the United States is establishing a new national security strategy and pursuing an active and proactive defense policy to implement it

[190] The United States has established four major defense objectives: 1) protecting the American homeland from enemy attack, 2) ensuring freedom of strategic access and action, 3) creating conditions for maintaining the international security order, and 4) strengthening alliances

[191] To achieve these objectives, the United States is building a "capabilitiesbased military force" based on the concept of 1) defending the American homeland, 2) deterring enemy threats in four key global regions, 3) maintaining military power capable of responding to potential simultaneous battlefields in two of these regions, and 4) securing the ability to achieve a decisive victory in one of the two regions

[192] In particular, in the operation of nuclear forces, the United States is moving beyond its traditional focus on deterrence and defense, and is not excluding the possibility of preemptive strikes and nuclear use against countries or terrorist organizations that threaten American security

[193] The United States continues to maintain its current troop strength of 1.4 million (10 Army divisions, 12 Navy carrier battle groups, 46 Air Force fighter squadrons, and 3 Marine divisions), while continuously pursuing military transformation and reorganizing its military structure into a brigade-centered Joint Task Force

[194] In line with the global US military redeployment plan, US military restructuring is also planned in Northeast Asia

[195] The US Forces Korea redeployment plan was agreed upon at the 2004 ROK-US Security Consultative Meeting, and the realignment of US Forces Japan is currently under discussion between the US and Japan

[196] The United States is currently discussing with the Japanese government plans to integrate the Fifth Air Force Command at Yokota Air Base, Japan, and the Thirteenth Air Force Command in Guam, thereby promoting efficient operations for US Air Forces in Japan

[197] The Army plans to establish a future combat system centered on 43 to 48 operational brigades (UAs) by pursuing transformations that simultaneously develop and improve current and future forces under the concept of "Rapid Decision Operations (RDO)" to conduct operations quickly and effectively before the enemy can react

[198] The Navy utilizes advanced information technology to simultaneously network dispersed warships to build strike capabilities

[199] RDO: Rapid and Decisive Operations Current Force: Current Army Forces for conducting current operations as part of the joint force Future Force

[200] Future Operational Forces planned to respond to the future security environment

[201] Unit Action Under the concept of “Non-Combat-Centered Warfare (NCW),” the Navy plans to form a force centered on an ESG (Embarkation Strike Group) of 37 Stryker combat vehicles

[303] North Korean Situation and Military Threats National Defense Commission Chairman Kim Jong-il focuses most of his public activities on military-related events, such as visits to military units

[304] He pursues internal unity and stability through the "military-first" policy, which emphasizes the military's political role

[305] While North Korea's economic situation has improved somewhat since 1999, food and energy shortages persist

[306] Due to the structural vulnerabilities of the socialist economic system, limitations in technology and capital, limited economic liberalization measures, and a lack of resources such as social infrastructure and energy, North Korea is facing difficulties in economic recovery

[307] Since the announcement of the "Economic Management Improvement Measures" in July 2002, North Korea has attempted economic reform measures, including the Kaesong Industrial Complex project

[308] It encompasses a complex set of principles: maintaining the regime and strengthening military power, leading economic development through the military, and disseminating military preferential treatment and revolutionary spirit throughout society

[309] Socially, following the June 15, 2000, inter-Korean exchange and cooperation projects that began in earnest, people-to-people contact and exchange have rapidly increased, leading to increased ideological education for the population

[310] B. Foreign Policy Since 2000, North Korea has shifted its foreign policy toward "pragmatic, all-round diplomacy" and has continuously pursued the normalization of relations with the West

[385] In November 2001 and July and August 2003, South Korean guard posts (GPs) were fired upon along the central and eastern fronts, and in February 2003, a MiG-19 aircraft violated the airspace over Yeonpyeong Island

[386] In accordance with the "Agreement on Preventing Accidental Clashes in the West Sea, Cessation of Propaganda Activities in the Military Demarcation Line Area, and Removal of Propaganda Materials" reached at the second inter-Korean general-level talks held on June 4, 2004, the two sides agreed to exchange information and issue warnings to illegal third-country fishing vessels starting June 15 and to remove visual media (propaganda materials, billboards, etc.) and loudspeaker broadcasting equipment installed in the frontline area

[387] However, North Korea, citing the South Korean government's refusal to allow a South Korean delegation to visit the North on the 10th anniversary of President Kim Il-sung's death, has refused to hold talks since July 2004 and has suspended the removal of propaganda materials from the frontline area

[388] Notably, even after the inter-Korean general-level talks, North Korean patrol boats have violated the Northern Limit Line (NLL) nine times, continuing to create tensions in the West Sea border area

[389] The post-Cold War global historical trend and the improvement in inter-Korean relations following the June 15th Inter-Korean Summit offer opportunities for establishing peace on the Korean Peninsula

[390] However, we still face various challenges

[391] The North Korean nuclear issue is the greatest threat to our security and a key issue hindering peace and stability in Northeast Asia

[392] The realignment of US Forces Korea in response to the US' shift in global strategy is impacting our overall security structure

[393] Furthermore, new security threats, including international terrorism and transnational crime, are emerging, posing a new challenge for us to proactively address

[394] To overcome these challenges and threats while also using them as opportunities for advancement, the government declared the "Peace and Prosperity Policy," which aims to promote peace on the Korean Peninsula and promote shared prosperity between the South and the North

[395] This policy aims to lay the foundation for peaceful unification and, furthermore, for coexistence and prosperity in Northeast Asia

[396] To achieve this, the government has articulated a national security policy encompassing unification, foreign affairs, and security policies

[397] National Interest and National Security Goals In his inaugural address, President Roh Moo-hyun presented the Peace and Prosperity Policy, which encompasses the basic direction of the Participatory Government's overall unification, foreign affairs, and security policies

[398] National interest is a value that a nation must pursue under any security environment, and is essentially identical to the national goal of pursuing national survival and prosperity

[399] Based on the Constitution of the Republic of Korea, the Participatory Government defined our national interests as five: "national security," "promotion of liberal democracy and human rights," "economic development and welfare," "peaceful unification of the Korean Peninsula," and "contribution to world peace and the common prosperity of humanity

[400] To realize these national interests amidst the pressing domestic and international security environment, the government has focused its national capabilities on establishing "peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula," "shared prosperity of South and North Korea and Northeast Asia," and "ensuring the safety of the people's lives" as national security goals

[401] The government has specified the following strategic keynotes that must be consistently maintained to achieve its national security goals, and has presented guidelines for policies in each field

[402] A. Promoting a Peace and Prosperity Policy The Peace and Prosperity Policy upholds the spirit of the Inter-Korean Basic Agreement and the June 15th Inter-Korean Joint Declaration, and its primary goal is to establish inter-Korean relations based on peaceful coexistence, reconciliation, and cooperation

[403] Furthermore, it seeks to foster shared prosperity and the formation of an economic community through the deepening and expansion of inter-Korean cooperation, and, based on these achievements, to build military trust and ease tensions between the two Koreas

[404] Furthermore, the government clearly states that it will firmly uphold the following principles in pursuing the Peace and Prosperity Policy

[405] First, it opposes war in any form and resolves all conflicts and pending issues peacefully through dialogue

[406] Second, it will pursue the principle of prioritizing mutual trust and reciprocity based on mutual recognition

[407] Third, all Korean Peninsula issues will be resolved through international cooperation based on the principle of inter-Korean parties

[408] Fourth, it will strive to be a "policy that works with the people" based on a national consensus

[409] Pursuing Balanced Pragmatic Diplomacy The balanced pragmatic diplomacy pursued by the government means achieving balance and strategic flexibility in policy decision-making and implementation to achieve security objectives

[410] This means simultaneously pursuing national interests alongside universal values such as peace, human rights, and sovereignty

[411] It also aims to develop multilateral security dialogue and cooperative policies alongside the ROK-US alliance, the foundation of security

[412] It actively responds to globalization trends while maintaining Korea's unique characteristics and status, and it establishes cooperative, horizontal, and mutually beneficial relationships in foreign relations

[413] Section 1: National Security Policy Concepts of the Participatory Government Chapter 2: National Security and Defense Policies of the Participatory Government C. Promoting Cooperative and Independent National Defense The government is pursuing cooperative and independent national defense, simultaneously securing self-defense capabilities and developing cooperative security relationships among nations, to establish a robust security posture that serves as the foundation for peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula

[414] This means developing the ROK-US alliance in a future-oriented manner, actively utilizing multilateral external security cooperation, and developing the capabilities and systems to play a leading role in deterring North Korea's provocations and, if they do occur, repelling them

[415] D. Comprehensive Security Today, each nation is strengthening its security capabilities across all sectors to respond not only to external military threats but also to emerging non-military threats both internally and externally, and to effectively address various security challenges

[416] To achieve the national security goal of "ensuring the safety of the people's lives from various security threats," the government is pursuing comprehensive security, an expanded security concept encompassing not only the military sector but also non-military sectors such as politics, economy, society, and the environment

[417] Strategic Tasks and Foundational Tasks The government establishes and implements strategic and foundational tasks based on national interests, national security objectives, and the national security strategic keynote

[418] Strategic tasks address key security issues and are crucial to achieving national security goals

[419] These are prioritized and pursued with tangible results during the Participatory Government's term

[420] Foundational tasks, while themselves security policy objectives, support the implementation of strategic tasks

[421] These ongoing tasks must be pursued consistently, not limited to a specific period

[422] The government's security plan, including these strategic and foundational tasks, is summarized in Table

[424] Our military is pursuing national security objectives and operational priorities to achieve them amidst a rapidly changing security environment and diverse defense conditions

[425] National Defense Objectives National Defense Objective: Protect the nation from external military threats and invasion, support peaceful unification, and contribute to regional stability and world peace

[426] Revised March

[427] First, "Protecting the nation from external military threats and invasion" refers to protecting the nation not only from direct military threats such as North Korea's conventional military forces, weapons of mass destruction, and forward deployment of military forces, but also from all external military threats that threaten our right to survival

[428] Second, "Supporting peaceful unification" means contributing to peaceful unification by deterring war on the Korean Peninsula, easing military tensions, and establishing peace

[429] Third, "contributing to regional stability and world peace" signifies our commitment to contributing to stability and peace in Northeast Asia by further enhancing friendly military cooperation with neighboring countries based on our national status and security capabilities

[430] Furthermore, we demonstrate our commitment to actively participating in the international community's efforts to maintain global peace, including UN peacekeeping operations

[431] Defense Operational Focus To achieve national security and national defense objectives, the Ministry of National Defense has established the following three priorities for defense operations: establishing a robust defense posture, promoting cooperative and independent defense, pursuing consistent defense reform, and establishing a trustworthy military image

[432] We are consistently pursuing these priorities while concentrating our military capabilities

[433] A. Establishing a Robust National Defense Posture Our military maintains a posture that deters enemy provocations and guarantees victory in the event of provocation by maintaining readiness to respond immediately to any military threat or invasion

[434] In particular, we are maintaining an operational readiness posture to maintain military stability in the Northwestern Sea Area, while establishing a response posture against North Korea's military and non-military provocations, including infiltration, localized provocations, and terrorism

[435] Meanwhile, we are devising various measures to prevent accidental conflicts between the South and the North, and are assessing the military impact of inter-Korean exchange and cooperation projects, such as the connection of the Gyeongui and Donghae Lines and the construction of the Kaesong Industrial Complex, and strengthening our military readiness posture

[436] Based on the ROK-US Combined Defense System, which plays a central role in deterring war on the Korean Peninsula, we are maintaining surveillance and information and early warning systems, developing a crisis management system and operational concepts to secure the safety of the Seoul Capital Area

[437] Through close consultations between the ROK and the US, we are pursuing the realignment of USFK forces and making various efforts to strengthen combined combat capabilities and operational readiness

[438] Furthermore, to respond to international terrorism, a new threat, we are developing contingency plans for each possible type of terrorism and maintaining a readiness posture

[439] We are also strengthening the cooperative system among counter-terrorism-related agencies, strengthening the security posture for key national facilities and US military installations in Korea, and enhancing specialized training for counter-terrorism operations units

[440] Furthermore, we are strengthening the morale of our soldiers to maximize intangible capabilities

[441] In particular, considering the recent changes in the security environment and the preferences of the new generation of soldiers, we are developing and systematically applying various morale-building programs and audio-visual materials to foster a sense of security and establish a sense of values as soldiers

[442] Section 2 Basic Direction of National Defense Policy Defense White Paper 49 Chapter 2 National Security Policy and Defense Policy of the Participatory Government [Defense White Paper B

[443] Promoting Cooperative Self-Reliant National Defense Self-reliant national defense and the ROK-US alliance are two critical pillars of our security

[444] As we develop independent capabilities for our own security, the ROK-US alliance can become more robust and future-oriented

[445] To implement the National Security Strategy, which pursues peace and prosperity on the Korean Peninsula, our military has established self-reliant national defense as a core element of national defense policy

[446] Following President Roh Moo-hyun's directive to "lay the foundation for self-reliant national defense within the term of the Participatory Government," the ROK military has established and is pursuing the "Cooperative Self-Reliant National Defense Promotion Plan

[447] Above all, the ROK-US alliance, which has crucially contributed to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula as the fundamental pillar of our security, is being developed to reflect recent changes in the strategic environment, such as the realignment of US Forces Korea

[448] Furthermore, we will prioritize rapidly expanding our deterrence capabilities against North Korea to proactively address existing military threats from North Korea, while gradually securing core capabilities to prepare for unspecified future threats, thereby laying the foundation for a practical, self-reliant national defense

[449] Furthermore, through ongoing military restructuring and strengthening the functions of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, we will establish a warfare system centered on the Joint Chiefs of Staff and lay the foundation for maximizing joint capabilities

[450] Furthermore, we will reorganize our military into an elite and efficient force suited to future warfare

[451] To smoothly promote cooperative, self-reliant national defense, it is crucial to build public consensus and continuously secure an appropriate defense budget

[452] Accordingly, the Ministry of National Defense is actively engaging in public relations efforts to garner public understanding and support, and is working closely with relevant ministries to secure the necessary defense budget, while taking the national economy into consideration

[453] Consistent Defense Reform Promotion The military is strengthening its military readiness and capabilities through continuous self-evaluation and reform to prepare for the ever-changing security environment and new challenges

[454] The Ministry of National Defense (MND) actively responds to the government's innovation efforts by selecting and actively pursuing reform initiatives across all defense sectors

[455] In particular, the Ministry will expand the civilian base by adjusting the active-duty structure of the MND Headquarters, thereby enhancing the expertise and efficiency of defense operations

[456] To improve the defense acquisition system and management system, reform initiatives will be identified through government-wide consultations

[457] The Defense Acquisition Program Administration (tentative name) will be established to integrate capabilities enhancement-related functions, thereby enhancing expertise, transparency, accountability, and efficiency in acquisition operations

[458] Through personnel system improvements, the Ministry will establish a fair and transparent personnel management and human resources management system and develop an education and training system to enhance the rationality and efficiency of personnel management

[459] To boost morale and well-being, we are improving the barracks environment and welfare conditions, including improvements to barracks facilities and military quarters, and enhancing the quality of life through various treatment improvements

[460] D. Establishing a Trustworthy Military No matter how powerful a military equipped with cutting-edge weapons and equipment, it can never achieve victory without the trust and support of the public

[461] To establish a trustworthy military, the military must first and foremost develop and establish a desirable military culture through internal reform

[462] To this end, we are fostering an advanced barracks culture that emphasizes autonomy and responsibility, while establishing a combat-oriented mindset and values

[463] Simultaneously, we are fostering a clean and transparent military culture through mental reform and various institutional improvements

[464] Furthermore, we will implement an "open national defense" that guarantees public participation, openness, and transparency

[465] In this regard, we will enhance the fairness, transparency, and customer orientation of military service administration

[466] We will actively disclose current defense issues and national concerns before the public demands them, while expanding the participation of civilian experts in the development of defense policy to gather diverse opinions from all walks of life

[467] Furthermore, we will implement a national defense system that actively protects and promotes the safety and interests of the people

[468] Specifically, we are establishing national disaster management support as the military's core mission and are reorganizing the organization and system to achieve this

[469] To protect the public's property rights resulting from various military activities, we are developing noise countermeasures at military airfields and firing ranges

[470] We are also strengthening our environmental management infrastructure by securing dedicated personnel for military environmental facility management and remediating contaminated soil

[471] Furthermore, we will do our utmost to proactively address various civil complaints to ensure the public's right to know and resolve any difficulties they may face

[473] To support this national effort, our military is deterring war through a robust ROK-U.S. combined defense posture

[474] We are developing military forces and operational plans to prepare for enemy armed provocations and are developing the capabilities to execute them

[475] In particular, following the realignment of US Forces Korea, we are pursuing the advancement of our military capabilities to expand our military's defensive role in South Korea's defense

[476] Our military must strengthen its deterrence against North Korea based on the ROK-US combined defense system, thereby making North Korea recognize the futility of its strategy of communizing unification through force

[477] Furthermore, we must foster military stability through mutual military trust-building and easing of tensions between the South and the North, and foster a favorable strategic environment through close military cooperation with neighboring countries

[478] This will deter enemy armed provocations and war on the Korean Peninsula

[479] Despite our efforts to deter war, if North Korea launches a military provocation, our military will repel the enemy's main force at the outset with the combined ROK-US forces, securing the safety of the Seoul metropolitan area and achieving unwavering victory

[480] To implement this strategic concept, our military has developed a ROK-US combined operational plan for defense purposes, anticipating North Korea's military provocations, and has established a perfect military readiness posture to execute it

[481] In particular, we will strengthen South Korea's defense role on the Korean Peninsula by promoting cooperative and independent national defense, and will review measures to strengthen the functions and organization of the Joint Chiefs of Staff for independent war planning, planning, and operational execution in the mid- to long-term

[529] FDO: Flexible Deterrence Option FMP: Force Module Package Reinforcement Forces The US reinforcement forces deployed to defend the Republic of Korea in the event of a crisis include approximately 690,000 troops, including the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps, approximately 160 ships, and approximately 2,000 aircraft

[530] These US reinforcements are deployed in the event of a crisis on the Korean Peninsula according to the "Time-Phased Force Deployment Data Plan (TPFDD)," which mostly includes the "Fast Deterrence Plan (FDO)" and the "Fighting Power Enhancement Plan (FMP

[531] The "Rapid Deterrence Plan" is a diplomatic, political, economic, and military measure implemented in a crisis prior to the outbreak of war, consisting of approximately 150 items

[532] Combat Power" "Increase" refers to a measure to reinforce key combat units and combat support units deemed essential in the early stages of war in case war deterrence through the "Rapid Deterrence Plan" fails

[533] This measure includes key forces such as rapidly deployed aircraft and carrier battle groups

[534] Reinforcement Forces, "TPFDD" US reinforcement forces are intended to be implemented within the framework of US military strategic maneuver

[535] Strategic maneuver refers to the transport of troops and equipment anywhere on the globe, encompassing transportation between theaters

[536] Key elements include air transport, ship transport, and the pre-positioning of equipment and war supplies to areas of potential conflict

[537] There are three types of US reinforcements

[538] First, there are forces based on the Flexible Deterrence Option (FDO

[539] This is a political, economic, diplomatic, and military plan aimed at deterring war, implemented in times of heightened war risk or crisis on the Korean Peninsula

[540] It consists of approximately 150 items, including surveillance and reconnaissance forces

[541] Second, there are forces based on the Force Module Package (FMP

[542] This plan reinforces key combat units and combat support units deemed essential in the initial stages of war in case deterrence through the FDO fails

[543] This includes carrier battle groups and other units

[544] Third, in the event of actual war, there are reinforcements based on the Time Phased Forces Deployment Date (TPFDD), which includes FDO and FMP forces

[545] This is divided into forces currently deployed on the Korean Peninsula (In-Place), forces scheduled for deployment in a timely manner (Pre-Planned), forces deployed additionally upon request (On-Call), and forces deployed overseas (Off-Peninsula

[546] These US reinforcements include forces to strike enemy artillery concentrated in the forward areas in the early stages of a conflict, several aircraft carrier battle ships equipped with the latest fighter jets and capable of three-dimensional maritime operations, air power for securing air superiority, air defense, and strikes on enemy territory, and forces to counter weapons of mass destruction

[547] The US's plan to deploy a massive reinforcement force—over 40% of the Navy, 50% of the Air Force, and 70% of the Marine Corps—in the event of a Korean conflict can be interpreted as a strong declaration of the US' commitment to the defense of the Korean Peninsula

[548] Defense White Paper 61 Chapter 3 Defense Posture for the Protection of Peace ㅇ Reconnaissance Satellite Defense White Paper Section 3 Military Readiness Posture of the ROK Military Despite positive changes in the security situation on the Korean Peninsula due to increased inter-Korean exchanges and cooperation, the threat posed by the North Korean military, which still possesses a numerical superiority over ours, remains unchanged

[549] Accordingly, while maintaining a robust ROK-US combined defense system to guard against the possibility of North Korean armed provocations, the ROK military is maintaining and developing a thorough military readiness posture to simultaneously respond to military threats such as North Korea's infiltration, localized provocations, and all-out war, as well as non-military threats such as terrorism

[550] Maintaining an Early Warning and Crisis Management System The ROK military monitors North Korean military activities 24 hours a day, utilizing its own signal and image collection system and ROK-US combined surveillance assets

[551] Utilizing various signal and image equipment, reconnaissance and surveillance equipment, the ROK military tracks and monitors the movements and training of key forces, including artillery, missile, and mechanized units, from the front lines to the rear areas

[552] Furthermore, automated surveillance equipment is used to monitor maritime and air activities in real time

[553] Meanwhile, in the event of detection of unusual signs of North Korean forces or a crisis on the Korean Peninsula, ROK-US joint crisis management and cooperation systems are being developed to effectively respond through close cooperation between ROK and US forces, thereby quickly ending crises and deterring war

[554] To this end, ROK and US are supplementing the peacetime Combined Crisis Management Consultative Body and developing specific response procedures for each potential crisis type

[555] They are continuously enhancing crisis management capabilities through regular exercises and frequent training

[556] Furthermore, the ROK and US are promoting the integration and performance improvements of the automated command center system to ensure prompt situational awareness and effective action by sharing information in a timely manner among the crisis response organizations of the Ministry of National Defense, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Combined Forces Command

[557] Our Military's Military Readiness Infiltration and Localized Provocation Readiness North Korea has committed relentless provocations against South Korea, including the 1996 Gangneung submarine infiltration, the 1999 Battle of Yeonpyeong, the 2001 territorial incursion of a North Korean merchant vessel, and the 2002 West Sea skirmish, as well as the Northern Limit Line (NLL) violations and the GP gunfire provocation

[558] Northern Limit Line In order to limit the patrol activities of the Navy and Air Force, the UN forces established a line in August

[559] Therefore, our military is strengthening patrol activities by ships, submarines, and aircraft in maritime jurisdictions, including the five northwestern islands

[560] In particular, we are strengthening our immediate response posture according to clear operational guidelines to prepare for intentional provocations in the northwestern waters

[561] Furthermore, we are reinforcing the demilitarized zone (DMZ) and coastal and riverine security postures with scientific surveillance equipment, and developing a response operational system to prepare for airspace violations

[562] The East Sea is defined by the Military Demarcation Line, and the West Sea by the median line between the five northwestern islands and North Korea

[563] GP: Guard Post A guard post installed within the DMZ

[564] Meanwhile, to establish an integrated defense posture across the civilian, government, and military sectors, the Integrated Defense Central Council was convened under the President in February 2004, where a resolution was adopted for total security

[565] We are also strengthening our operational posture in rear areas, including evacuation and decontamination in preparation for chemical weapons attacks, protection of urban infrastructure, and facility restoration

[566] Full-scale War Readiness Our military is establishing a permanent combat readiness posture to counter North Korea's military threats

[567] Specifically, in the event of a North Korean provocation, we are developing an operational concept to strike and quickly eliminate the enemy's core forces, leveraging ROK-US combined intelligence and precision strike capabilities

[568] This will allow us to quickly eliminate the threat to the Seoul metropolitan area in the early stages of a war

[569] Under this operational concept, we are enhancing our warfighting capabilities through various combined and joint exercises, such as the Ulchi Focus Lens (UFL), the Combined Reinforcement of Operations (RSOI), and the Foal Eagle (FE

[570] Furthermore, to overcome North Korea's numerical superiority, our military is independently developing and deploying the Korean-type large destroyer (KDX-II), the K1A1 main battle tank, the Shingung, and the Cheonma, as part of efforts to secure qualitative capabilities

[571] We are also continuously developing automated command centers, utilizing cutting-edge computer equipment, to effectively command operations

[572] To address the North Korean chemical, biological, and radiological threat, which poses a significant threat to us, we are continuously developing our chemical, biological, and radiological operational capabilities, including the establishment of the ROK Army Chemical, Biological, and Radiological Defense Command in 1999, significant reinforcement of chemical units and equipment, early deployment of US chemical, biological, and radiological units, continued acquisition of civilian gas masks, and formation of emergency response units to prepare for toxic gas accidents in urban areas

[573] Ulchi Focus Lens RSOI

[574] The process of accepting, staging, forward movement, and integrating US reinforcements arriving at the operational area based on the time-based unit deployment plan, transforming the force into a combat force capable of meeting the commander's operational requirements

[575] Chapter 3 Defense Posture for the Protection of Peace V. Terrorism Preparedness

[576] In the post-Cold War era, the international community faces new and diverse forms of terrorist threats, as evidenced by the September 11 attacks

[577] No country is immune from these threats

[578] Terrorism Preparedness Training for Specialized Units. The ROK military, in preparation for hosting the 2002 World Cup and Asian Games, implemented a comprehensive development plan for terrorism preparedness

[579] This plan was supplemented and the preparedness posture was further developed, including the formation of a specialized terrorism unit, the strengthening of counter-terrorism organizations, and the reinforcement of equipment

[580] To prepare for chemical, biological, and radiological terrorism, we have expanded the organization and equipment for reconnaissance and decontamination missions under the Armed Forces Chemical, Biological, and Radiological Defense Command

[581] We are also strengthening specialized training for specialized counter-terrorism units, explosive and contamination accident disposal teams, and sniper operatives

[582] At the same time, we are developing a close cooperative system with relevant counter-terrorism agencies, such as the National Intelligence Service and the National Police, to prevent any form of terrorism in advance and to enable a rapid joint response should an incident arise

[595] Combined and Joint Exercises and Training A. Ulchi Focus Lens (UFL) Exercise ROK-US Joint UFL Exercise UFL

[596] Ulchi Focus Lens The Ulchi Focus Lens (UFL) exercise is a comprehensive command post exercise for the defense of the Republic of Korea, conducted annually in August

[597] It integrates the "Ulchi Exercise," which provides government-level military support, and the "Focus Lens Exercise," which aims to master operational planning procedures at the military level

[598] Since 1976, this annual ROK-US joint exercise has been conducted using computer simulation methods

[599] The government exercise, which takes place during the Ulchi Focus Lens exercise, involves not only administrative agencies but also major industries, conducting government-wide war preparedness training

[600] The military, through joint ROK-US crisis management and defense exercise procedures, enhances combat readiness and joint operational capabilities

[601] B. Combined Wartime Augmentation (RSOI) Exercise The Combined Wartime Augmentation (RSOI) exercise is a command post exercise conducted to familiarize US reinforcement forces, who will be deployed to the Korean Peninsula during wartime, with the procedures for their initial arrival on the peninsula, their forward movement, and their integration into the battlefield, as well as the ROK military's support procedures for wartime support, mutual logistics support, mobilization, and restoration of combat power

[602] The Combined Wartime Augmentation Exercise is held annually in March and involves the ROK Ministry of National Defense, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, headquarters of each service, units above the level of operations commander, US Forces Korea, and US augmentation units

[603] D. Exercise Foal Eagle (FE

[604] The Foal Eagle (FE) exercise is a combined and joint field maneuver exercise conducted to enhance ROK-US combined and joint air, land, and sea operations, combined special operations, and rear operations capabilities

[605] This exercise involves the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Combined Forces Command, and each operational command

[606] It has been conducted annually in October since 1961, but since 2002, it has been conducted in March in conjunction with the Combined Wartime Augmentation (RSOI) exercise

[607] The first part of the exercise involves defense operations for key rear area facilities, combined amphibious operations, and combined air and air operations

[608] The second part involves a corps-level field training exercise (FTX), including a Marine landing team

[609] Taegeuk Exercise Taegeuk Exercise is a Command Post Exercise (CPX) that has been conducted annually in May since 1996 to cultivate the Joint Chiefs of Staff's war planning and planning capabilities and enhance operational command capabilities in preparation for wartime

[610] Through the Taegeuk exercise, the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) masters wartime missions and functional execution procedures, strengthens combat-oriented thinking and jointness, and develops a joint operation execution system, large-scale power warfare, and deep-sea operations

[611] Hoguk Exercise is a large-unit field training exercise (FTX) conducted annually since 1996 under the supervision of the Operations Command under the supervision of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[612] This exercise aims to enhance the operational execution capabilities of corps-level units and enhance the capabilities of large-unit joint operations and integrated combat

[654] Defense White Paper Chapter 3: National Defense Posture for the Protection of Peace Defense White Paper Section 5: Mobilization and Homeland Defense Operational Posture Today, advanced nations are focusing their standing forces on critical and essential forces to efficiently manage their defense resources, while gradually increasing the proportion of reserve forces

[655] Future warfare on the Korean Peninsula is expected to be a total war, mobilizing all national resources

[656] Therefore, the efficient operation of reserve forces will be a critical factor in determining the outcome of the war

[657] Therefore, considering limited defense resources and the mobilization environment, the ROK military is establishing an effective wartime mobilization posture to secure elite reserve forces aligned with the direction of building a standing force

[658] It is also strengthening its ability to conduct homeland defense operations, while promoting mobilization activities with a focus on reserve resource management and the development of education and training

[659] Wartime Mobilization Posture A. Personnel Mobilization Personnel mobilization includes troop mobilization, wartime labor call-up, and technical personnel mobilization

[660] Troop mobilization refers to the mobilization of troops required for military unit expansion (increase or creation) or replacement of losses during wartime, incidents, or when a mobilization order is declared, and their use as combat personnel for military units

[661] Troop mobilization is a key element accounting for the majority of personnel mobilization

[662] To ensure the efficiency of troop mobilization during wartime, we are continuously improving resource management, troop escort, and control systems

[663] Wartime labor mobilization refers to the mobilization of personnel to perform labor tasks, such as transporting supplies and ammunition, in support of military operations

[664] To efficiently manage and operate wartime labor mobilization, the "Wartime Labor Mobilization Operation Regulations" were enacted to establish procedures for performing tasks

[665] Furthermore, wartime workers, previously dispersed across mobilization units, were integrated into wartime labor units, ensuring operational flexibility

[666] Technical personnel mobilization refers to the mobilization of personnel holding technical qualifications to operate or maintain equipment

[667] This mobilization program, which previously designated 235 types of national technical qualifications and licenses, is being expanded to include approximately 30 types of advanced technologies and licenses in new technology and information technology fields

[668] B. Material Mobilization Material mobilization is the timely and appropriate mobilization of resources, including supplies, equipment, facilities, and businesses, held by both the public and private sectors, to support military operations and ensure war sustainability

[669] Depending on the resource being mobilized, it is categorized into industrial mobilization, transportation mobilization, construction mobilization, and communications mobilization

[670] Industrial mobilization involves mobilizing items that meet military specifications, such as food, clothing, oil, and construction materials, as well as production and maintenance companies, public relations media, and hospitals

[671] The Ministry of National Defense is exploring ways to relax military specifications and utilize civilian materials instead

[672] To ensure efficient resource management, it is expanding and operating an industrial mobilization information system across relevant units and departments

[673] Transport mobilization involves the use and control of transportation equipment, such as automobiles, ships, and aircraft, as well as maintenance companies, transportation, and handling companies, required by the military in times of emergency

[674] To ensure timely mobilization, mobilization methods have been improved, including the use of substitute vehicles for some insufficient vehicles and the expansion of the scope of designated substitutes by vehicle type in resource-scarce areas

[675] Construction mobilization involves the use or control of buildings, land, construction equipment, construction equipment maintenance companies, and construction companies needed by the military

[676] To shorten mobilization times, improvements have been made to designate similar equipment as replacements when equipment is in short supply in a given city or province

[677] Communication mobilization involves the use or control of general communications (international and domestic lines), satellite communication lines, and information and communications companies

[678] It strives to quickly support the military communications network during wartime and ensure the success of operations

[679] Mobilizing for a certain period of time and returning equipment to its original owner after demobilization

[680] This applies to equipment mobilization

[681] Controlled Operation Controls the production, repair, processing, and distribution processes necessary to achieve the mobilization objective

[682] Except for the controlled areas, autonomy of the business is guaranteed, and applies to business mobilization, etc

[684] Since its establishment on April 1, 1968, the Republic of Korea Reserve Forces have been mobilized 89 times over the past 30 years, with approximately 4 million personnel

[685] They have killed 85 infiltrating spies and armed guerrillas and captured

[686] To strengthen the system for conducting homeland defense operations in both wartime and peacetime, the reserve forces have been mobilized annually to participate in counter-infiltration operations

[687] They have also modernized military combat equipment and replenished supplies

[688] Furthermore, the "Regulations on the Development and Support of Homeland Reserve Forces," which stipulate support responsibilities and support items for each reserve force development entity, systematic development plans, and work procedures, have been enacted and implemented to establish an institutional framework for ensuring support for homeland defense operations

[689] Reserve Forces Resource Management Regional reserve forces units play a central role in managing reserve forces and supporting homeland defense operations in their respective areas of responsibility

[690] Regional reserve forces are organized at the town, township, and ward level nationwide, while separate mobile units are organized and operated at the city, county, and district level

[691] Workplace reserve forces units are organized from brigades to squads based on the number of reserve forces in their respective workplaces

[692] Commanders of general workplaces with reserve forces at the company level or higher, and of national security-targeted organizations and facilities with reserve forces at the squad level or higher, are required to organize reserve forces

[693] Recently, an internet-based reserve force resource management and daily accounting system was established between regional Military Manpower Administrations and reserve force units

[694] Reserve force units at all levels now receive 18 computerized lists necessary for reserve force resource management, including the status of reserve force resources, transfers and departures, departures and returnees, and newly assigned members and those with status changes

[695] This has increased the efficiency of related tasks

[696] Reserve Forces Training Reserve force training aims to "familiarize soldiers with mobilization procedures and ensure post-mobilization combat capability" and to cultivate capabilities for homeland defense operations

[697] The Ministry of National Defense is continuously improving and developing the training system to enhance the level and intensity of training while ensuring the livelihoods of the people, enabling immediate combat capability

[698] The system was improved to include first-year reservists, who previously only underwent four-hour annual muster drills, in mobilization training

[699] Furthermore, the mobilization training period was adjusted from three nights and four days to two nights and three days

[700] Furthermore, the exemption from training, previously limited to eighth-year conscripts, was expanded to cover seven years of service

[701] This alleviated the burden of military service on the Korean people

[702] Furthermore, by maintaining designated mobilization units and conducting mobilization training, the system was improved to enhance overall combat capabilities

[717] Current Status and Challenges of Our National Defense Section 1 The Concept and Direction of Cooperative Self-Reliant Defense Section 2 Future-Oriented Development of the ROK-US Alliance Section 3 Development of External Military Relations Section 4 Easing Tensions and Establishing a Peace Regime on the Korean Peninsula Section 5 Building Self-Reliant Defense Capabilities Section 6 Promoting Welfare to Improve the Quality of Life Section 7 Mid-Term Plans and Defense Budget Chapter 4 Current Status and Challenges of Our National Defense Section 1 The Concept and Direction of Cooperative Self-Reliant Defense Cooperative self-reliant defense refers to developing the complementary ROK-US alliance based on our self-reliant defense capabilities

[718] The government has designated the "parallel development of the ROK-US alliance and self-reliant defense" as one of three strategic tasks for achieving national security goals and is concentrating its capabilities on a nationwide level

[719] Accordingly, the Ministry of National Defense has established a "Cooperative Self-Defense Promotion Plan" to implement the President's strategic directives and is focusing on strengthening self-defense capabilities in conjunction with the future-oriented development of the ROK-US alliance

[720] Strategic Tasks that address key security issues and are crucial to achieving national security goals are prioritized and pursued with tangible results during the Roh Moo-hyun administration

[721] Since the founding of the ROK-US alliance, we have maintained a strong ROK-US alliance

[722] While the methods and extent of our efforts have varied depending on changes in domestic and international conditions, such as the security environment, available national defense resources, and public interest, we have continued our efforts toward self-defense

[723] Our efforts to achieve self-reliant national defense began in earnest in 1971, amidst heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula, including the rapid buildup of military power driven by North Korea's "Four Major Military Guidelines," the 1968 raid on the Blue House by armed guerrillas, and the hijacking of the USS Pueblo

[724] The reduction of US forces in Korea was underway

[725] Under the banner of self-reliant national defense, our military continued to pursue the Yulgok Project until the early 1990s, securing basic defense capabilities and strengthening the operational capabilities of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

[726] In 1994, we reclaimed peacetime operational control, achieving remarkable results in strengthening our military power, operational capabilities, and the development of a combined command system

[727] However, following the economic crisis of the 1990s, the downward trend in defense spending continued, and the military threat from North Korea's weapons of mass destruction and other asymmetrical forces increased

[728] Consequently, South Korea has not yet maintained the military power to proactively deter North Korea

[729] This has contributed to security vulnerabilities, as evidenced by the widespread anxiety about security in some sectors of society whenever there is a change in the Republic of Korea-United States alliance

[730] Furthermore, amidst growing public expectations for the ROK-US alliance to develop in line with our national strength, the need to expand the ROK military's defense role has grown to proactively address changes and challenges in the security environment, such as North Korea's nuclear development and the realignment of US Forces Korea

[731] Concept and Direction of Cooperative Self-Defense The Participatory Government's pursuit of cooperative self-defense is an expression of the nation's will to become a key player in the security of the Korean Peninsula, responding to the demands of the times and public expectations

[732] This commitment was officially declared by President Roh Moo-hyun in his 2003 Liberation Day address and his Armed Forces Day address

[733] August 15th Commemorative Address: "During my term, within the next ten years, I intend to lay the foundation for our military to acquire self-defense capabilities

[734] B. Concept of Cooperative Self-Defense The basic concept of cooperative self-defense is to develop the ROK-US alliance and actively utilize external security cooperation, including military cooperation and collective security systems with neighboring countries, while developing the capabilities and systems to play a leading role in deterring North Korea's provocations and repelling them if they do occur
